'''Joseph Berkson''' (14 May 1899 – 12 September 1982)<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2531346 | jstor=2531346 | title=Obituaries | last1=O'Fallon | first1=Judith Rich | last2=Cormack | first2=R. M. | last3=Bithell | first3=J. F. | journal=Biometrics | year=1983 | volume=39 | issue=4 | pages=1107–1111 }}</ref> was an American biostatistian, who is best known for having identified a source of bias in [[observational study|observational studies]] caused by selection effects. This bias eventually became known as [[Berkson's paradox]].<ref>{{cite journal | pmid=21001024 | year=1946 | author1=BERKSON J | title=Limitations of the application of fourfold table analysis to hospital data | journal=Biometrics | volume=2 | issue=3 | pages=47–53 | doi=10.2307/3002000 | jstor=3002000 }}</ref>

Berkson was trained as a physicist (BSc 1920, [[City College of New York|College of City of New York]] (CCNY), M.A., 1922, Columbia), physician (M.D., 1927, Johns Hopkins), and statistician (Dr.Sc., 1928, Johns Hopkins).<ref name="Biostatistics">O'Fallon WM (1998). "Berkson, Joseph". Armitage P, Colton T, Editors-in-Chief. ''Encyclopedia of Biostatistics.'' Chichester: John Wiley & Sons. Volume 1, pp. 290-295.</ref>

==Works and views==
In 1950, as Head (1934–1964) of the Division of Biometry and Medical Statistics<ref name="Biostatistics"/> of the [[Mayo Clinic]], [[Rochester, Minnesota]], Berkson wrote a key paper entitled ''Are there two regressions?''<ref>{{cite journal|author=Berkson J|title=Are there two regressions?|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|year=1950|volume=45|pages=164–180|doi=10.2307/2280676|issue=250|jstor=2280676 }}</ref> In this paper Berkson proposed an error model for [[regression analysis]] that contradicted the [[classical error model]] until that point assumed to generally apply and this has since been termed the [[Berkson error model]]. Whereas the classical error model is statistically independent of the true variable, Berkson's model is statistically independent of the observed variable.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Heid IM, Kuchenhoff H, Miles J, Kreienbrock L, Wichmann HE |title=Two dimensions of measurement error: Classical and Berkson error in residential radon exposure assessment|journal=J Expo Anal Environ Epidemiol|year=2004|volume=14|pages=365–377|doi=10.1038/sj.jea.7500332|pmid=15361895|issue=5|doi-access=}}</ref> Carroll et al. (1995) refer to the two types of error models as follows:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Carroll |first1=R. J. |last2=Ruppert |first2=D. |last3=Stefanski |first3=L. A. |title=Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models |publisher=Chapman & Hall |location=London |edition=Second |year=2006 |isbn=1-4200-1013-1 |pages=26–32 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9kBx5CPZCqkC&pg=PA26 }}</ref>
* ''error models'' including the Classical Measurement Error models and Error Calibration Models, where the conditional distribution  of ''W'' given (''Z'',&nbsp;''X'') is modeled — use of such a model is appropriate when attempting to determine ''X'' directly, but this is prevented by various errors in measurement.
* ''regression calibration models'' (also known as controlled-variable or [[Berkson error models]]), where the conditional distribution of ''X'' given (''Z'',&nbsp;''W'') is modeled.<!-- Since no attempt is made to explain what X, Y, and Z are, these two bullet points are incomprehensible. -->

Berkson is also widely recognised as the key proponent in the use of the [[logistic distribution|logistic]] in preference to the [[normal distribution]] in probabilistic techniques.<ref name="Sussex">Lecture notes for Economics students at Sussex university. Online resource: [http://www.sussex.ac.uk/Units/economics/Logistics/gss_lec1.doc]{{dead link|date=April 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He is credited with the introduction of the [[logit]] model in 1944,<ref>{{cite journal|author= Berkson J|title=Application of the logistic function to bio-assay|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|year=1944|volume=39|pages=357–65|doi= 10.2307/2280041|issue= 227|publisher= Journal of the American Statistical Association, Vol. 39, No. 227|jstor= 2280041}}</ref> and with coining this term. The term was borrowed by analogy from the very similar [[probit]] model developed by [[Chester Ittner Bliss]] in 1934.

Berkson was a prominent opponent of the idea that cigarette smoking causes cancer. In the 1957 [[Liggett & Myers]] annual report, he was quoted as saying "the evidence, taken as a whole, does not establish, on any reasonable scientific basis, that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer."<ref>{{cite book|title=TobaccoDocuments.org|url=http://tobaccodocuments.org/profiles/people/berkson_joseph.html/|archive-url=https://archive.today/20071224060407/http://tobaccodocuments.org/profiles/people/berkson_joseph.html/|url-status=dead|archive-date=2007-12-24}}</ref>  Following the issuance of the famous report ''[[Smoking and Health: Report of the Advisory Committee to the Surgeon General of the Public Health Service]]'', he was quoted in [[Life magazine|''Life'' magazine]] as saying it was "very doubtful that smoking causes cancer of the lung."<ref>{{cite journal|title=Verdict on Cigarets: Guilty as Charged|journal=Life Magazine|date=January 24, 1964|pages=52–64|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-lMEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA56|publisher=Time Inc|author1=Inc, Time}}</ref>
